opus-5.5.text:
I think when people look at AI from the outside, it seems incredibly complicated: huge models, enormous compute, all these papers coming out every day, all these tricks and techniques. But if you step back and look at what has actually driven progress over the past decade or so, the core ideas are surprisingly few and surprisingly simple.

Roughly, you have a very general architecture, you have a lot of data, you have a lot of compute, and you have a simple objective, like predicting the next token, or getting a reward signal through reinforcement learning. Then you scale it up. Most of the progress comes from doing these simple things really well and at a much larger scale, not from some very clever, intricate design.

Coming from a physics background, this actually felt quite familiar to me. In physics you hope the underlying laws are simple and elegant, and the complexity you see in the world emerges from those simple rules. AI feels similar. The behavior of these models is extremely rich, sometimes surprising, but the recipe that produces them is not that complicated. A lot of very smart people have spent years building elaborate, hand-designed systems, and again and again those get overtaken by simpler methods that scale better. That's the "bitter lesson," in a sense.

So when I say AI is fundamentally simple, I don't mean it's easy. The engineering is extremely hard: making training stable, getting the data right, building the infrastructure, finding the right environments for RL. Those take enormous effort. But the conceptual core is simple. And I think that's important for researchers to keep in mind. If you find yourself building something very complicated, it's often a sign you haven't found the right abstraction yet. Usually the thing that works in the end is the simpler idea that you just push much further than people expected.

r001.rationale: It explains simplicity through a general architecture, data, compute, simple objectives, and scaling, but does not connect it to the ability to run experiments.

r002.rationale: It does not state that understanding physical theory at a given energy scale requires experimental data at that scale.

r003.rationale: It says the core ideas are few and simple, but does not argue that AI research has a backlog of ideas to test rather than having exhausted ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
I think when I say AI is simple, I mean it in a few layers.

The first layer is that the core ideas are actually very few. If you look at what drives progress today, it's basically: you have a lot of data, you have a lot of compute, you have a model that's general enough, and you have an objective that scales. Pretraining is next-token prediction. Reinforcement learning is "try something, see if it works, do more of what works." These are ideas a smart undergraduate can understand in an afternoon. What's hard is not the idea, it's believing in it long enough and executing at scale.

The second layer is that the field has been going through a process of simplification rather than complication. When I was doing my PhD, every task had its own architecture, its own inductive biases, its own tricks. Question answering had one model, summarization had another, games had another. Now it's one model, one training recipe, and the task is just a prompt. ReAct is a good example of this. The whole idea is that reasoning and acting can be the same thing, you just generate a thought and then generate an action, in the same stream of tokens. People at the time thought agents needed planners, memory modules, all these components. It turned out that a lot of that complexity was unnecessary if the language model is good enough.

The third layer, and this is maybe the more philosophical point, is that I think intelligence itself might be simple. Not simple to build, but simple in principle. Evolution didn't design the brain with a very complicated blueprint. It found a general learning mechanism and scaled it. So when people ask me "what's the secret," I always say there isn't really a secret. The bitter lesson is the lesson. The things that look complicated right now, like agents, tool use, long-horizon tasks, I think in a few years they'll also look simple in hindsight, because we'll have found the right objective and the right environments to learn from.

Of course "simple" doesn't mean "easy." Running an experiment that costs tens of millions of dollars is not easy. But the conceptual core, I think, is much smaller than it looks from the outside, and I think that's actually good news for the field.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments can be expensive and distinguishes execution from conceptual simplicity, but it does not explain AI’s simplicity in terms of the ability to run experiments.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss physical theory, energy scales, or the need for experimental data at a given scale.

r003.rationale: It describes AI’s core ideas as few and says complexity may simplify in hindsight; it does not argue that AI research has a backlog of ideas to test rather than an exhaustion of ideas.

astra-6.text:
I mean that a lot of complexity can emerge from a relatively simple underlying mechanism. With AI, you have a model, an objective, and a process for learning from data. The behavior you get can be incredibly rich, even though the basic recipe is fairly compact.

Take language modeling. The training task is to predict the next token. That sounds very simple. But to do it well across many different contexts, a model benefits from learning about language, facts, and patterns of reasoning. So the simplicity of the objective doesn’t imply simplicity of the resulting behavior.

Of course, building these systems is difficult. There’s a huge amount of engineering involved, and we still don’t fully understand why they work as well as they do. So by “fundamentally simple,” I don’t mean that AI is easy or that everything is solved. I mean that we may not need to explicitly design every capability. A simple learning process, applied at sufficient scale, can produce much more than we put into it by hand.

r001.rationale: The response describes a simple learning objective and process, but does not explain simplicity in terms of the ability to run experiments.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss physical theories, energy scales, or the experimental data needed to understand them.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize AI research as having ideas left to test or contrast that with an exhaustion of ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean that the basic ideas behind AI can be surprisingly simple, even when the behavior that emerges is very complex. You define a model, give it data, and optimize an objective. For a language model, that objective might simply be predicting the next token. Yet doing that well can require learning something about language, knowledge, and reasoning.

Of course, simple doesn’t mean easy. Making that process work at scale takes enormous engineering effort, and we still don’t fully understand why certain capabilities emerge. But I think it’s useful to distinguish the simplicity of the underlying recipe from the complexity of the system it produces.
